---
title: "NVIDIA NIM Embeddings"
guide-section: "Building a Store"
---

[NVIDIA NIM](https://build.nvidia.com/nvidia) is NVIDIA's platform for serving AI models, and it includes a set of embedding models tuned for retrieval. Those models can be used in two ways: through NVIDIA's hosted API, or by running NIM containers on your own GPUs. The second option is what makes NIM interesting for many teams, since it lets you keep documents and queries entirely on infrastructure you control while still getting GPU-accelerated embeddings.

raghilda supports both setups through `EmbeddingNVIDIA`. This guide covers getting an API key, choosing a model, pointing the provider at a self-hosted container, and handling inputs that are too long for the model.

## Installation

There's nothing extra to install. NIM exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, and `EmbeddingNVIDIA` talks to it with the `openai` client library that already comes with raghilda.

To use NVIDIA's hosted API, create an account at [build.nvidia.com](https://build.nvidia.com/nvidia), generate an API key, and set it in the environment:

```bash
export NVIDIA_API_KEY="nvapi-..."
```

The provider reads `NVIDIA_API_KEY` automatically. You can also pass `api_key=` directly, but the environment variable is preferable because raghilda doesn't store the key with the store's configuration (more on that below).

## Basic usage

With the key in place, creating a provider looks like this:

```{python}
#| eval: false
from raghilda.embedding import EmbeddingNVIDIA

provider = EmbeddingNVIDIA(model="nvidia/llama-nemotron-embed-1b-v2")
```

Pass it to a store with the `embed=` argument:

```{python}
#| eval: false
from raghilda.store import DuckDBStore
from raghilda.embedding import EmbeddingNVIDIA

store = DuckDBStore.create(
    location="my_store.db",
    embed=EmbeddingNVIDIA(),
)
```

`DuckDBStore.create()` embeds a short probe string to work out the size of the model's vectors, so any problem with the key or the model name surfaces immediately.

## Choosing a model

NVIDIA's catalog changes fairly often, so it's best to browse [build.nvidia.com](https://build.nvidia.com/search?q=embed) for the current list. A few retrieval-focused models to start with:

| Model | Notes |
|---|---|
| `nvidia/llama-nemotron-embed-1b-v2` | The default. A compact, general-purpose retrieval model with multilingual support |
| `nvidia/nv-embedqa-e5-v5` | An English model tuned for question-answering retrieval |
| `nvidia/nv-embedqa-mistral-7b-v2` | A larger 7B-parameter model for higher-quality English retrieval |

Each model's page on build.nvidia.com lists its vector size and maximum input length. You can also check the vector size directly by embedding something:

```{python}
#| eval: false
provider = EmbeddingNVIDIA(model="nvidia/nv-embedqa-e5-v5")
print(len(provider.embed(["test"])[0]))
```

::: {.callout-note}
A store is tied to the model it was created with, because vectors from different models can't be compared with each other. Changing models means creating a new store and re-ingesting.
:::

## How query and document embeddings work

Like Cohere, NVIDIA's retrieval models embed queries and documents differently. NVIDIA's API calls these two modes `"query"` and `"passage"`, and raghilda maps `EmbedInputType.QUERY` and `EmbedInputType.DOCUMENT` onto them. The store handles this for you: chunks written with `upsert()` or `ingest()` are embedded as passages, and the text you give to `retrieve()` is embedded as a query.

If you're calling the provider directly, pass the input type yourself:

```{python}
#| eval: false
from raghilda.embedding import EmbeddingNVIDIA, EmbedInputType

provider = EmbeddingNVIDIA()

doc_embeddings = provider.embed(
    ["HNSW is a graph-based approximate nearest-neighbor index."],
    input_type=EmbedInputType.DOCUMENT,
)

query_embedding = provider.embed(
    ["How do vector indexes work?"],
    input_type=EmbedInputType.QUERY,
)
```

When `input_type` is left out, the provider assumes `EmbedInputType.DOCUMENT`.

## Self-hosted NIM containers

NVIDIA publishes Docker images that serve NIM models on your own hardware. Once a container is running, point the provider at it with `base_url=`:

```{python}
#| eval: false
from raghilda.embedding import EmbeddingNVIDIA

provider = EmbeddingNVIDIA(
    model="nvidia/llama-nemotron-embed-1b-v2",
    base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1",
)
```

The `model` should match the model the container is serving. A self-hosted container doesn't check API keys, but the underlying OpenAI client won't start without *some* key. The simplest fix is to set `NVIDIA_API_KEY` to any placeholder value in the environment where you run raghilda:

```bash
export NVIDIA_API_KEY="not-used"
```

Using the environment variable here (rather than `api_key=`) matters when you reconnect to the store later, since the key isn't saved with the store. The `base_url` *is* saved, so a reconnected store will keep sending requests to your container.

See [NVIDIA's NIM documentation](https://docs.nvidia.com/nim/) for instructions on pulling and running the containers.

## Handling long inputs

Every embedding model has a maximum input length. By default (`truncate="NONE"`), NVIDIA's API rejects any input that's longer than the model allows, and the error is raised during ingestion. If you'd rather have long inputs cut down to size, set `truncate="END"`, which drops tokens from the end of the text until it fits:

```{python}
#| eval: false
provider = EmbeddingNVIDIA(truncate="END")
```

Truncation is convenient, but it means the end of a long chunk won't influence its embedding. If you find yourself relying on it a lot, it's usually better to make your chunks smaller. See [Chunking](chunking.qmd) for how to adjust chunk sizes.

## Batching and rate limits

`EmbeddingNVIDIA` sends texts in batches of 20 by default. You can change this with `batch_size=`. A larger batch means fewer requests, and that can help with throughput on a self-hosted container that has GPU memory to spare.

If the API returns a rate-limit error (HTTP 429), the provider backs off and retries. It waits one second at first and doubles the wait after each attempt (up to 60 seconds), then gives up after about three minutes in total. Other errors are raised right away.

## Reconnecting to a store

When you connect to an existing store, raghilda rebuilds the provider from the configuration saved at creation time. That configuration includes the model, `base_url`, batch size, and truncation setting:

```{python}
#| eval: false
from raghilda.store import DuckDBStore

store = DuckDBStore.connect("my_store.db")
```

As mentioned above, the API key is never saved, so `NVIDIA_API_KEY` needs to be set when you reconnect.

## Parameters

`EmbeddingNVIDIA` takes five parameters. All of them are optional, so with `NVIDIA_API_KEY` set in the environment you can use NVIDIA's hosted API without passing any arguments:

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `model` | `"nvidia/llama-nemotron-embed-1b-v2"` | NVIDIA embedding model name |
| `base_url` | `"https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1"` | API endpoint. Change this for a self-hosted NIM container |
| `api_key` | `None` | API key. Falls back to the `NVIDIA_API_KEY` environment variable |
| `batch_size` | `20` | Texts per API call |
| `truncate` | `"NONE"` | What to do with over-long inputs: `"NONE"` raises an error, `"END"` truncates |

The ones you're most likely to change are `model`, `base_url` (when using a self-hosted container), and `truncate`. Everything except `api_key` is saved with the store, so a reconnected store talks to the same endpoint with the same settings. For the full API details, see the [`EmbeddingNVIDIA` reference page](/reference/embedding.EmbeddingNVIDIA.qmd).

## Complete example

This example builds a small store from two web pages using a question-answering model, then searches it:

```{python}
#| eval: false
from raghilda.store import DuckDBStore
from raghilda.embedding import EmbeddingNVIDIA
from raghilda.read import read_as_markdown
from raghilda.chunker import MarkdownChunker

store = DuckDBStore.create(
    location="docs.db",
    embed=EmbeddingNVIDIA(model="nvidia/nv-embedqa-e5-v5", truncate="END"),
    name="docs",
    title="My Documentation",
    overwrite=True,
)

chunker = MarkdownChunker()
for url in ["https://example.com/doc1", "https://example.com/doc2"]:
    store.upsert(chunker.chunk(read_as_markdown(url)))

store.build_index()

chunks = store.retrieve("How do I configure authentication?", top_k=5)
for chunk in chunks:
    print(chunk.text[:200])
```

To run the same pipeline against a self-hosted container, the only change is adding `base_url=` to the provider. The rest of the code stays the same.

## Using NVIDIA with ChromaDB

ChromaDB doesn't have a built-in NVIDIA embedding function, so when you pass `EmbeddingNVIDIA` to `ChromaDBStore`, raghilda wraps it in an adapter. The adapter still uses the right input type for queries and documents, and the provider is restored when you reconnect from Python. The one limitation is that ChromaDB clients in other languages won't be able to use the collection's embedding function. See [ChromaDB Embedding Functions](chromadb-embedding-functions.qmd) for details.

## When to use NVIDIA NIM

`EmbeddingNVIDIA` is a good choice when:

- you want embeddings to stay on your own infrastructure but still run on GPUs
- you're already running other NIM models and want to keep your stack consistent
- you want hosted retrieval models with separate query and document embeddings

If you don't have GPUs to run containers and would still like to keep data local, [SentenceTransformers](embedding-sentence-transformers.qmd) and [Ollama](embedding-ollama.qmd) both run comfortably on a laptop.
